how-to-pin-a-github-action-to-a-commit-s.text:
← Pinned Actions Check

How to pin a GitHub Action to a commit SHA

Most workflow steps look like this:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

v4 is a tag, and a tag is just a name someone attached to a commit — the action's maintainer (or anyone who compromises their account) can move it to point at a different commit at any time. Pinning to a commit SHA instead means the reference cannot be silently changed: a SHA is the commit.

1. Find the commit SHA a tag currently points to

Use git ls-remote against the action's repository. No clone is needed, and this makes only the same kind of request your own git fetch already makes:

git ls-remote https://github.com/actions/checkout refs/tags/v4

That prints a line like:

8f152de45cc393bb48ce5d89d36b731f54556e65	refs/tags/v4

The first column is the commit SHA. If the tag has no matching commit under refs/tags/, try refs/heads/<name> instead — some actions reference a branch (@main) rather than a version tag.

2. Replace the tag with the SHA

Keep the original tag as a trailing comment, so a human reading the workflow still knows which version it is without decoding the hash:

- uses: actions/checkout@8f152de45cc393bb48ce5d89d36b731f54556e65 # v4

That line now resolves to exactly one commit, forever. Upgrading later is a deliberate, reviewable diff: look up the SHA for a newer tag and replace both the hash and the comment.

3. Do this for every third-party action, in every workflow

A workflow can have several jobs, each with several steps, each `uses:`-ing a different action — and a single unpinned reference is enough to be the weak link. Paste your workflow YAML into Pinned Actions Check to find every mutable reference across every workflow file at once, each with its own ready-to-run git ls-remote command, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any third-party action is still referenced by a tag or branch instead of a commit SHA — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added unpinned action before it merges.

Why this matters: it has already happened

In March 2025, the widely used tj-actions/changed-files action had its version tags repointed at a malicious commit that dumped CI secrets into workflow logs. Any workflow referencing it by tag (@v35, and similar) ran that malicious code the next time it triggered. A workflow that had pinned to a commit SHA was never affected by the retag, because its reference could not be moved.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. Confirm any commit SHA yourself before pinning to it, and verify before relying on the output. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and it does not tell you whether the code at that commit is itself safe to run — only which commit a tag currently resolves to.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. Free, experimental, may move or go offline without notice.

Everything on the linked tool runs in your browser; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool makes no network calls of its own.

PINNED ACTIONS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Are your GitHub Actions pinned to a commit SHA?

A third-party action referenced by a tag (@v4) or branch (@main) trusts whatever code that ref points to right now — and its owner can repoint it at different code tomorrow. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds every uses: line that isn't pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA, with the exact command to look up the SHA yourself.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own — not even to look up the SHA for you.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineActionRefStatusFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any mutable (unpinned) action is found

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added unpinned action before it merges.

Common questions

Why is pinning a GitHub Action to a tag like @v4 a risk?

A tag or branch name is mutable: the action's owner — or an attacker who compromises their account — can repoint it at a different commit at any time. The next time your workflow runs, it runs whatever code that tag now points to, with whatever permissions and secrets your workflow has. A full 40-character commit SHA cannot be silently repointed, which is why GitHub's own hardening guidance recommends it.

Has this actually happened?

Yes. In March 2025 the widely used tj-actions/changed-files action had its version tags repointed at a malicious commit that dumped CI secrets into logs in any workflow that referenced it by tag. Workflows that had pinned it to a commit SHA were unaffected by the retag.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. For every mutable reference it finds, it prints the exact git ls-remote command you can run yourself to look up what that ref currently resolves to. The lookup, and the decision to pin, stay entirely yours.

Does a clean scan mean my repository is secure?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented thing: whether third-party uses: references are pinned to a commit SHA. It is not a security audit, and it makes no claim about your repository's overall security or compliance posture.

What about actions in my own repository?

References starting with ./ (a local composite or JavaScript action in the same repository) and docker:// (a container image reference) are skipped — neither is the third-party supply-chain risk this tool exists to catch.

More: how to pin a GitHub Action to a commit SHA. Already run OpenSSF Scorecard? See how this checker compares for the pinning question specifically.

It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee that your CI is safe from supply-chain attacks, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including confirming any commit SHA yourself before pinning to it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.py from the repo and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The YAML you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Pinned SHAs stop a mutable tag from being swapped out from under you, but they don't catch every risk in a workflow: Actions Injection Check flags pwn-request checkouts and script-injection from untrusted ${{ github.event }} expressions, Actions Permissions Check flags workflows and jobs with no explicit permissions: grant or with write-all, Actions Cache Poisoning Check flags an actions/cache write reachable from a fork trigger or an unscoped restore-keys fallback, and Actions Secret Leak Check flags a step that transforms a secret before it can be masked, or exports one to $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_OUTPUT without ::add-mask:: — four more slices of a hardened CI setup. The same mutable-tag-vs-pinned-reference question applies past CI, too: Docker Base Image Pin Check asks it of a Dockerfile's FROM line instead of a workflow's uses: line. A pinned, permission-scoped workflow can still leave branch protection stuck: Required Checks Drift Check flags a required status check name a renamed job, a removed job, or a dropped pull_request trigger has left nothing can ever satisfy again. And a workflow that is pinned, permission-scoped and green can still put the wrong revision live: Deploy Concurrency Check flags the ways two runs of a deploy workflow are allowed to overlap, so the one that finishes last -- not the newer one -- is what is deployed. A reference this tool marks pinned is pinned only at that one hop — Actions Transitive Pin Check fetches what a pinned reusable workflow or composite action itself loads and flags it if that is unpinned underneath, a gap this tool's own "no network calls" design cannot see into. To run all of these as one GitHub Action on every pull request, add Workflow Audit.

Want this check and 21 others in one pass? devsec-toolkit runs it alongside the rest of the portfolio's devsec checks (GitHub Actions, Docker, Compose, Kubernetes, supply chain, code, AI-agent configs) over a whole repository, with one report, SARIF for code scanning and a baseline so CI fails only on new findings.

Free and open source. If this saved you from shipping a supply-chain gap, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-openssf-scorecard.html.text:
← Pinned Actions Check

Pinned Actions Check vs. OpenSSF Scorecard

Different shapes of tool for an overlapping question. Scorecard scores 18 dimensions of a repository's supply-chain security -- pinning is one of them -- using the GitHub API and a token, usually wired into CI. This page runs only the pinning question, on one workflow file you paste, free, with no token, no install, and no network call of its own.

What each tool is for

OpenSSF Scorecard is an open-source project (github.com/ossf/scorecard) that runs 18 named checks against a repository -- among them Branch-Protection, Code-Review, Dangerous-Workflow, Token-Permissions, Vulnerabilities, and Pinned-Dependencies -- and scores each 0 to 10. Its Pinned-Dependencies check, by Scorecard's own documentation, looks at whether a project's build and release pipeline is pinned to immutable references across several ecosystems (GitHub Actions, Dockerfile base images, and downloaded-script installs among them), and returns one aggregate score rather than a line-by-line list. Running it needs a GitHub token to avoid API rate limits, and it is typically run through the ossf/scorecard-action in CI or read from Scorecard's own public dataset of already-scanned open-source repositories.

This checker does one narrower thing: you paste the YAML of a GitHub Actions workflow file, and it lists every third-party uses: line that is not pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA -- file, line, the mutable reference it found, and the exact git ls-remote command to look up the SHA yourself. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no GitHub token and no install, and makes no network call of its own, so it works the same on a private repository's workflow, an unpushed fork, or a file from a repo you do not administer.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
How does my whole repository score across 18 supply-chain dimensions, tracked over time?OpenSSF Scorecard -- that is its entire job, and this tool does not attempt it.
Which exact lines in one workflow file are an unpinned third-party action, and what do I run to fix each one?This checker -- a file:line list with a copy-pasteable remediation command, not a score.
I need this to work on a private repository's workflow, or a file I have not pushed anywhere.This checker -- no token, no repository access, nothing leaves your browser. Scorecard's public dataset and default setup target public repositories.
I want pinning checked across Dockerfiles and package-manager installs too, not just GitHub Actions.OpenSSF Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies check covers more ecosystems than this tool does; this tool is GitHub Actions uses: lines only.
I want this wired into CI to block a merge automatically.Either: Scorecard's own GitHub Action, or this tool's check.py --fail-on-risk for the pinning question specifically.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run Scorecard for the ongoing 18-dimension score and still reach for this tool the moment the question is "which line, right now, and what do I paste to fix it" on a file that is not yet in a public, tokened CI run.

Run the free pinned-actions check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or OpenSSF Scorecard?

They are different shapes of tool for an overlapping question. Scorecard is a broader, ongoing measurement: it runs 18 named checks against a repository -- Branch-Protection, Code-Review, Dangerous-Workflow, Token-Permissions, Vulnerabilities, Pinned-Dependencies, and more -- each scored 0 to 10, using the GitHub API and a token, usually wired into CI or read from Scorecard's own public dataset of already-scanned open-source repositories. This tool answers only the one question in its name: are the third-party actions in the workflow YAML you paste pinned to a commit SHA. You paste the file, it runs in your browser, and it needs no token, no install, and no repository access, because it never talks to GitHub at all. If you want an ongoing score across 18 dimensions of a public repository's supply-chain posture, Scorecard is the right tool. If you want a fast, private, no-setup answer to one specific question about one workflow file -- including a private repository's, since nothing here is fetched or uploaded -- this is the narrower tool for that.

Does Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies check do the same thing as this tool?

Not exactly. Scorecard's own documentation describes Pinned-Dependencies as scoring how much of a project's build and release pipeline is pinned to an immutable reference, and by its own account that check looks across multiple ecosystems -- GitHub Actions, Dockerfile base images, and downloaded-script installs among them -- and returns one 0-to-10 score for the repository as a whole, not a line-by-line list. This tool checks exactly one of those surfaces, GitHub Actions uses: lines, and instead of a score it lists every unpinned reference individually with the file, line, and the exact git ls-remote command to look up the commit SHA yourself. Running both is not redundant: Scorecard's score can move for reasons that have nothing to do with your workflow files, and this tool's line-level list does not tell you how your repository compares to any baseline.

Why would I need a token-free, no-install checker if Scorecard already exists?

Three reasons this tool exists alongside it. First, Scorecard's CLI needs a GitHub token to avoid API rate limits in practice, and its GitHub Action needs to run inside your CI with repository access -- this tool needs neither, so it works on a workflow file from a private repository, a fork you have not pushed anywhere, or a repo you do not administer, with nothing leaving your browser. Second, Scorecard is a Go binary (or a container image) you install and configure; this tool is a page you open. Third, when the answer you actually want is "which lines, and what do I run to fix them," a 0-to-10 score is a worse fit than a list of file:line findings with a copy-pasteable remediation command, which is the only thing this tool produces.

Is this page affiliated with OpenSSF or the Scorecard project?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Open Source Security Foundation or the Scorecard project. Scorecard is an open-source project of the OpenSSF, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from Scorecard's own public documentation and source repository at github.com/ossf/scorecard.

It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee that your CI is safe from supply-chain attacks, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including confirming any commit SHA yourself before pinning to it. vs-reading-the-workflow-yaml-by-hand.htm.text:
← Pinned Actions Check

Pinned Actions Check vs. reading the workflow YAML by hand

This page names no company or product — reading a workflow file before trusting it is a habit most maintainers already have, not a competing tool. The gap is not carelessness: an abbreviated commit SHA looks pinned at a glance, and telling it apart from a full 40-character one is exactly the kind of check a quick read is bad at.

What a manual read catches reliably

An obvious @v4, @main, or @master on a short, single-job workflow — a version tag or a branch name reads as clearly not a commit SHA. Those are the cases a reviewer scanning top to bottom notices without much effort, and this tool does not replace that kind of reading.

What a manual read struggles with, and why

Where the two diverge on a real repository.
CaseReading by handThis checker
An abbreviated SHA, e.g. @a1b2c3dReads as pinned at a glance — it is clearly not a tag or branch nameClassified as mutable: only a full 40-character SHA cannot be silently repointed, and this tool applies that rule the same way every time
A version tag that looks numeric, e.g. @v4.1.2Easy to mistake for "specific enough" since it names an exact releaseClassified as mutable — the tag itself can still be repointed by its owner, unlike a commit SHA
A repository with a dozen workflow files, several jobs eachChecking every uses: line in every file is repetitive and exactly the kind of check attention degrades acrossScans every pasted file identically; line forty gets the same treatment as line one
Local actions (./path) and Docker referencesEasy to flag as unpinned by mistake, since they carry no SHA at allClassified separately as local / docker, never counted as a mutable finding

None of this is about attention or diligence. A 7-character hex string and a 40-character one are both "not a tag", and only the length tells them apart — a distinction that is trivial for a regex and easy to skip while scanning by eye.

Run the free pinned-actions check

When to still read the file yourself

This tool answers one narrow question: is a given uses: reference pinned to a commit SHA. It does not tell you whether the code at that commit is itself safe, it makes no network call, and it resolves nothing on your behalf — for every mutable finding it prints the exact git ls-remote command so you can look up and judge the current commit with your own network access, which is still a job for you.

Common questions

What does reading a workflow file by hand catch reliably?

An obvious @v4, @main, or @master sitting in a short, single-job workflow -- a version tag or branch name is easy to recognise as not a commit SHA. Those are the cases a reviewer scanning the file top to bottom notices without much effort, and this tool does not replace that kind of reading.

Why is an abbreviated SHA the case a manual read misses?

Because it looks pinned. A reference like some-action@a1b2c3d is not a version tag or branch name, so a quick glance reads it as safe -- but a 7-character abbreviation is not what this tool, or GitHub's own supply-chain hardening guidance, counts as pinned: it can still collide with another commit, and only a full 40-character SHA cannot be silently repointed. Telling a 7-character hex string from a full 40-character one, correctly, on line thirty of a long file, is exactly the kind of check attention is worst at sustaining.

Does file count matter, or is this only about one confusing line?

Both. A repository with a dozen workflow files, each with several uses: lines, turns a pinning review into checking every reference in every file for the difference between a full SHA, an abbreviated one, and a tag that happens to look numeric. A tool that classifies every pasted line the same way does not get less careful on file twelve than it was on file one.

Does a clean scan mean the code at that commit is safe?

No. This tool answers one narrow question -- is this uses: reference pinned to a fixed commit -- and does not evaluate what that commit contains. It makes no network call and resolves nothing on your behalf; for a mutable finding it prints the exact git ls-remote command so you can look up and judge the current commit yourself.
